findings.issue_text: pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/impl.go:87 — Caching a device before a successful store update makes a rejected device's next request skip the limit check and authenticate.
pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/anonstore/database.go:110 — The unlocked count-then-upsert lets concurrent new device requests all observe spare capacity and insert past the configured cap.
pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/impl.go:119 — A client can omit the untrusted device ID header and make tagging return success without ever checking the configured cap.

pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/client.go:49 — Any counting or persistence failure other than the sentinel is logged and authentication succeeds, so database failures silently disable limit enforcement.

packages/grafana-runtime/src/config.ts:97 — anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined` on GrafanaBootConfig is inferred as type `undefined` while the GrafanaConfig interface declares `number | undefined`, and the constructor's `merge(this, defaults, options)` actually overwrites it with a real server-provided number at runtime, so the concrete class's static type is unsound relative to its own runtime contract.

pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/impl.go:87 — tagDeviceUI caches the device key via localCache.SetDefault before CreateOrUpdateDevice succeeds, so once ErrDeviceLimitReached is returned once, subsequent requests from the same device within the 29-minute cache TTL hit the cache and return nil, silently bypassing the device limit and letting anonymous auth succeed without ever persisting/re-checking the device

pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/anonstore/database.go:109 — CreateOrUpdateDevice checks CountDevices and then inserts in two separate, non-transactional DB calls, creating a TOCTOU race where concurrent requests near the limit can each pass the count check and all insert, exceeding deviceLimit

pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/client.go:44 — Authenticate() now calls TagDevice synchronously on every anonymous request (was fire-and-forget in a goroutine), so every anon page load blocks on a DB round trip (and a COUNT query when device limit is set) instead of returning immediately

pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/client.go:44 — Removing the goroutine's dedicated 2-minute timeout context means TagDevice now runs under the caller's request context, so a slow/contended DB directly increases latency (or causes failures) for every anonymous authentication request, with no isolation from the auth request path

pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/client.go:44 — TagDevice now runs synchronously on the request's own ctx with no bounded timeout, so a slow/hung DB blocks every anonymous authentication request instead of the previous fire-and-forget goroutine with a 2-minute timeout that degraded gracefully.

pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/client.go:44 — Removing the goroutine's defer recover() means a panic inside TagDevice/tagDeviceUI/CreateOrUpdateDevice now propagates directly out of Authenticate(), risking a crashed/500'd request instead of being safely logged and swallowed as before.

pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/anonstore/database.go:74 — CreateOrUpdateDevice/updateDevice issue DB calls using the caller-supplied ctx with no per-call timeout applied anywhere in the anon store, so if the underlying DB stalls the query can block for as long as the (possibly unbounded) upstream context allows, whereas before it was capped at 2 minutes.

pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/client.go:44 — Anonymous.Authenticate now hard-fails authentication with ErrDeviceLimitReached, which is trivially triggerable by any client sending arbitrary, unsigned X-Grafana-Device-Id header values to exhaust the device cap and deny anonymous access to legitimate users (DoS via unauthenticated request)

pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/impl.go:124 — Device identity used for the new limit/enforcement logic (X-Grafana-Device-Id) is entirely client-supplied and unvalidated/unsigned, so the device count/limit mechanism can be trivially inflated or bypassed by spoofing arbitrary device IDs

pkg/api/frontendsettings.go:198 — AnonymousDeviceLimit is exposed to unauthenticated users via public frontend settings, giving an attacker the exact threshold needed to efficiently exhaust the device cap and trigger the anonymous-auth DoS

pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/anonstore/database_test.go:51 — The only limit test stops at the store, so it misses that a failed over-limit tag remains cached and the same device is accepted on retry.
pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/anonstore/database_test.go:62 — The sequential test misses the non-atomic count-then-insert race that lets concurrent first-time devices exceed the configured cap.

pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/anonstore/database_test.go:69 — The test never verifies that an existing active device can still be refreshed at capacity, leaving the new update-only success branch untested.

pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/client.go:44 — Authenticate() changed from async fire-and-forget to synchronous with ErrDeviceLimitReached now failing anonymous auth, but there is no client_test.go at all exercising Authenticate, so this behavioral change has zero test coverage

goldens.comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.

Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/impl.go:87 — Caching a device before a successful store update makes a rejected device's next request skip the limit check and authenticate.
pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/anonstore/database.go:110 — The unlocked count-then-upsert lets concurrent new device requests all observe spare capacity and insert past the configured cap.
pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/impl.go:119 — A client can omit the untrusted device ID header and make tagging return success without ever checking the configured cap.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff for impl.go, the TagDevice function at line 119 shows the flow: it gets the device key, checks local cache, then calls tagDeviceUI. The tagDeviceUI function calls a.anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice which does check the device limit (as shown in database.go). The finding claims a client can omit the device ID header to bypass the cap check, but examining the code flow: if no device ID is provided, getDeviceKey would generate one based on IP/user-agent. The device limit check happens in CreateOrUpdateDevice regardless of how the device ID was obtained. The finding misreads how the code works - the limit check is in the database layer, not dependent on whether a header was provided.

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/client.go:49 — Any counting or persistence failure other than the sentinel is logged and authentication succeeds, so database failures silently disable limit enforcement.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that in client.go lines 44-51, when TagDevice returns an error that is NOT ErrDeviceLimitReached, the code logs a warning but continues to return a successful authentication (returns the anonymous identity). This means if the database fails during CountDevices or CreateOrUpdateDevice, the limit enforcement is bypassed. However, this is arguably intentional design - failing open for availability rather than blocking anonymous access on transient DB errors. It's a valid architectural concern about the security/availability tradeoff, but not necessarily a bug since the behavior appears deliberate.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/grafana-runtime/src/config.ts:97 — anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined` on GrafanaBootConfig is inferred as type `undefined` while the GrafanaConfig interface declares `number | undefined`, and the constructor's `merge(this, defaults, options)` actually overwrites it with a real server-provided number at runtime, so the concrete class's static type is unsound relative to its own runtime contract.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims there's a type unsoundness issue, but this is incorrect. In TypeScript, `undefined` as a value is assignable to `number | undefined` type. The class property `anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined` will have its type inferred as `undefined`, but since the class implements `GrafanaConfig` interface which declares `anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined`, TypeScript will ensure type compatibility. The runtime behavior of `merge()` overwriting the value with a number is perfectly valid since `number` is part of the union type. This is standard TypeScript behavior and not a bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/client.go:44 — Authenticate() now calls TagDevice synchronously on every anonymous request (was fire-and-forget in a goroutine), so every anon page load blocks on a DB round trip (and a COUNT query when device limit is set) instead of returning immediately

pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/client.go:44 — Removing the goroutine's dedicated 2-minute timeout context means TagDevice now runs under the caller's request context, so a slow/contended DB directly increases latency (or causes failures) for every anonymous authentication request, with no isolation from the auth request path

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the diff removes the goroutine with a dedicated 2-minute timeout context (lines 44-56 in the old code) and replaces it with a synchronous call using the request context (lines 44-50 in the new code). This is a real architectural change that could affect latency for anonymous authentication requests. However, this appears to be an intentional design decision to properly handle the ErrDeviceLimitReached error (which requires synchronous execution to return the error to the caller). The finding raises a valid concern about the tradeoff, but it's not a bug - it's a scope/architecture concern about the change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/client.go:44 — TagDevice now runs synchronously on the request's own ctx with no bounded timeout, so a slow/hung DB blocks every anonymous authentication request instead of the previous fire-and-forget goroutine with a 2-minute timeout that degraded gracefully.

pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/client.go:44 — Removing the goroutine's defer recover() means a panic inside TagDevice/tagDeviceUI/CreateOrUpdateDevice now propagates directly out of Authenticate(), risking a crashed/500'd request instead of being safely logged and swallowed as before.

adjudication.rationale: The diff clearly shows that in client.go, the previous implementation wrapped TagDevice in a goroutine with a defer recover() block that caught panics and logged them as warnings. The new code removes this goroutine and recover(), calling TagDevice directly in the Authenticate method. If TagDevice or any of its downstream calls (like CreateOrUpdateDevice) panic, the panic will now propagate up through Authenticate, potentially crashing the request handler. This is a real behavioral change that could cause 500 errors instead of graceful degradation.

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/anonstore/database.go:74 — CreateOrUpdateDevice/updateDevice issue DB calls using the caller-supplied ctx with no per-call timeout applied anywhere in the anon store, so if the underlying DB stalls the query can block for as long as the (possibly unbounded) upstream context allows, whereas before it was capped at 2 minutes.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that in client.go, the previous code created a goroutine with a 2-minute timeout context (`newCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), timeoutTag)`) before calling TagDevice. The new code removes this goroutine and timeout, calling TagDevice directly with the caller's context (`a.anonDeviceService.TagDevice(ctx, httpReqCopy, anonymous.AnonDeviceUI)`). The database operations in anonstore/database.go (CreateOrUpdateDevice, updateDevice, CountDevices) use the passed context without any internal timeout. This means DB operations that were previously capped at 2 minutes can now block indefinitely if the upstream context has no timeout, which is a behavioral regression that could cause request hangs.

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/client.go:44 — Anonymous.Authenticate now hard-fails authentication with ErrDeviceLimitReached, which is trivially triggerable by any client sending arbitrary, unsigned X-Grafana-Device-Id header values to exhaust the device cap and deny anonymous access to legitimate users (DoS via unauthenticated request)

pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/impl.go:124 — Device identity used for the new limit/enforcement logic (X-Grafana-Device-Id) is entirely client-supplied and unvalidated/unsigned, so the device count/limit mechanism can be trivially inflated or bypassed by spoofing arbitrary device IDs

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the device ID used for limit enforcement comes from client-supplied headers (X-Grafana-Device-Id). Looking at the diff, the device limit logic in database.go uses device.DeviceID for counting and enforcement, and this ID originates from client requests. While this is a valid security/architecture concern about the new limit feature being bypassable, it's not strictly a bug in the diff's implementation - the code does what it's designed to do. It's an important design consideration for the new device limit feature that the diff introduces. The concern is real and grounded in the diff's new functionality.

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/api/frontendsettings.go:198 — AnonymousDeviceLimit is exposed to unauthenticated users via public frontend settings, giving an attacker the exact threshold needed to efficiently exhaust the device cap and trigger the anonymous-auth DoS

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows AnonymousDeviceLimit being added to FrontendSettingsDTO (line 195 in frontend_settings.go) and exposed via getFrontendSettings (line 198 in frontendsettings.go). Frontend settings are typically accessible to unauthenticated users. The diff also shows ErrDeviceLimitReached error being returned when the device limit is reached (anonstore/database.go), and this error propagates up through the authentication flow (client.go lines 44-47). Exposing the exact device limit value allows an attacker to know precisely how many devices they need to create to exhaust the limit and trigger denial of service for anonymous authentication. This is a legitimate security concern - information disclosure that aids in a DoS attack.

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/anonstore/database_test.go:51 — The only limit test stops at the store, so it misses that a failed over-limit tag remains cached and the same device is accepted on retry.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real gap in test coverage. Looking at the diff, when TagDevice fails with ErrDeviceLimitReached in client.go (line 44-47), the error is returned but the local cache in impl.go may have already cached the device key before the store operation failed. The test in database_test.go:51-68 only tests the store layer directly, not the full flow through AnonDeviceService which includes the localCache. This is a valid concern about incomplete test coverage for the caching behavior when device limits are exceeded, though it's not a bug per se - it's a missing integration test for an edge case.

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/anonstore/database_test.go:62 — The sequential test misses the non-atomic count-then-insert race that lets concurrent first-time devices exceed the configured cap.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a real race condition in the implementation. Looking at the diff in database.go lines 103-113, the CreateOrUpdateDevice function first calls CountDevices() and then conditionally inserts. This count-then-insert pattern is not atomic, so concurrent requests could both pass the count check and exceed the device limit. The test in database_test.go only tests sequential operations (one device created, then another attempted), not concurrent scenarios. This is a valid architectural concern about the implementation, though it's more of a missing test/incomplete edge-case handling rather than a bug in the test itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/anonstore/database_test.go:69 — The test never verifies that an existing active device can still be refreshed at capacity, leaving the new update-only success branch untested.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a gap in test coverage. Looking at the test `TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit` (lines 51-68), it only tests the case where a NEW device is rejected when the limit is reached (ErrDeviceLimitReached). However, the new `updateDevice` method (lines 72-99) has a success path where an existing device within the expiration window gets updated. The test doesn't verify that an existing device can be successfully refreshed when at capacity - it only verifies that a completely new device is rejected. This is a legitimate missing test case for the new update-only logic branch.
